thesis: Selective overweight: structural copper deficit and central-bank gold demand outweigh a correcting gold tape and a deteriorating iron ore complex. Own copper producers first, quality gold second, avoid bulk-commodity pure plays.
markdown:
## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
**OVERWEIGHT (selective)** over 12 months. The metals complex is bifurcating: copper retains a structural demand story (electrification, grid, AI data-center buildout) even as prices retreat from record highs; gold remains structurally supported by central-bank buying despite a volatile correction from January's $5,597/oz record; iron ore faces a multi-year downtrend on Chinese property weakness. Positioning: copper producers first (FCX), quality gold majors on the pullback (NEM), underweight bulk-commodity (iron ore) pure plays.

## MACRO & COMMODITY BACKDROP
**Copper (as of early July 2026)**: Futures pulled back toward ~$6.00/lb, a two-week low, as Middle East escalation strengthened the USD and clouded the global manufacturing outlook. Goldman Sachs expects prices to decline somewhat from record highs in 2026 but remain historically elevated. A second-order supply risk has emerged: Strait of Hormuz disruption has lifted sulfuric acid (used in copper refining) to ~$820/t in the Middle East and ~$1,200/t in import regions like Brazil, pressuring producer costs. Chinese buyers — roughly 60% of global copper demand — have been actively buying the dip.

**Gold (as of July 10, 2026)**: Spot ~$4,104/oz, up ~$858 YoY but well below the all-time high of $5,597/oz set January 29, 2026. The multi-year rally has entered a volatile correction phase, yet remains structurally supported by central-bank demand and geopolitical fragmentation. Large-cap producer AISC of $1,400–1,600/oz leaves historically wide margins even after the correction.

**Iron ore / bulks**: The World Bank expects iron ore prices to decline further through 2026–27, falling below 2019 levels. Chinese domestic steel demand continues to contract on ongoing property-market weakness.

**China**: Growth slowing, property weak, deflationary pressure and overcapacity persist; stimulus remains the key upside swing factor for industrial metals demand.

## SUB-SECTOR DYNAMICS
**Copper producers**: Best structural story in the complex — electrification, grid capex, and AI infrastructure demand against a thin project pipeline. Sector leadership: BHP (~$180B), Rio Tinto (~$140B), Freeport-McMoRan (~$82B), Glencore (~$92B).

**Gold producers**: Record free cash flow at spot prices (Newmont generated an all-time record $3.1B of FCF in Q1 2026 alone). Equities have lagged bullion, leaving valuation support; consolidation and capital returns are the theme. Primary large-caps: Newmont (~$102B), Agnico Eagle, Barrick.

**Diversified / bulks**: Iron ore exposure is the drag — the structural China property story argues for underweighting pure iron ore leverage; diversified majors (BHP, RIO) are held up by their copper and aluminum growth capex (e.g., RIO's $1.5B AP60 low-carbon aluminum smelter commissioned May 2026).

## VALUATION
Miners broadly trade below historical mid-cycle EV/EBITDA on spot-annualized earnings, reflecting market skepticism that spot copper and gold prices hold. That skepticism is the opportunity in copper (deficit math) and the risk in bulks (China structural decline). Gold majors trade at material discounts to consensus targets (NEM consensus $139 vs ~$95 spot) — the street is paid to be patient.

## RISK ASSESSMENT
**Macro risks**: A deeper China downturn (no stimulus response), sustained USD strength, and a global manufacturing recession would hit the entire complex. Middle East escalation cuts both ways — bullish gold, bearish industrial demand.
**Sector risks**: Cost inflation (acid, energy, labor), resource nationalism (Indonesia, Latin America), permitting delays on new supply.
**Positioning risk**: Metals equities are high-beta to the commodity; size the sleeve at 4–8% with single names 1–4%.
